summary: The essay argues that national festivals around the world, long expressions of cultural identity, are being eroded by commercialization, tourism, and social media, which turn traditions into packaged spectacles. It supports this with dated quotes from artists, organizers, curators and academics in Ireland, Mexico, Thailand, Australia, India and Sicily. It concludes that festivals must balance commercial success with authenticity, through audience education and a return to the genuine spirit of the traditions.
one_line: An essay arguing that commercialization, tourism and social media are hollowing out national festivals, and that authenticity and audience education are needed to preserve them.
key_facts: On October 15, 2023, at the "Festival of Heritage" in Limerick, Ireland, 75-year-old weaver Eileen O'Connell said the festival is now "more of a show for those with cameras and less of heritage."
On September 5, 2023, the Mayor of New Orleans cited a record increase in tourist spending during Mardi Gras.
On November 2, 2023, during Dia de los Muertos in Mexico, Oaxaca artist Carlos Mendez said tourists come to see a spectacle and worried locals are "forgetting it ourselves."

At Thailand's Loi Krathong festival on November 12, 2023, organizer Somchai Poomlard said the sentiment is lost amid selfie sticks and staged photo ops, serving an "Instagram aesthetic rather than our ancestors."

Melbourne cultural anthropologist Emma Richardson spoke at a symposium on September 21, 2023 and described a 'Disneyfication' in which complex cultural expressions are reduced to amusement park attractions.
On March 8, 2024, at India's Holi festival, New Delhi social media analyst Aarav Singh said Holi's spiritual and historic roots get overshadowed by the spectacle.
Sicily festival curator Gianna Vasquez called on September 30, 2023, at a conference on cultural preservation, for "a festival renaissance that honors the genuine spirit of our traditions."
The essay says festivals risk becoming standardized experiences packaged for consumption rather than vehicles for cultural transmission.
Festival organizers caught in a cycle of funding and profit may prioritize international audiences over the needs of the culture itself.
Social media can amplify cultural practices but can also dilute profound expressions into clichéd hashtags.
The essay proposes educating tourists about the history and significance of festivals so they become participants in preservation rather than passive onlookers.
The essay frames the future of festivals as a tightrope between commercial success and cultural authenticity, risking 'theme park renditions of our past.'
